paper_title: Probing Phenomenological Experiences Through Electroencephalography Brainwave Signals In Neuroarchitecture Study
venue: International Journal of Built Environment and Sustainability
abstract: Experiences are a part of our daily lives through our interactions with the environment around us. We live life through the realm of experiences, be it playing or working. As we encounter phenomena frequently, it is deduced that most of it comes from within the built environment, considering how most of our time is spent indoors. Hence, it is imperative that we understand the impact of the built environment on human physiology especially within the context of religious spaces which is largely attributed to phenomenological experiences. Despite the importance of understanding the impact of the built environment on human physiology, phenomenological studies that addresses this relationship are still lacking. This presents a gap which necessitates evidence to be provided in the form of phenomenological studies. Hence, this study attempts to address the gap by utilising evidential data with the utilisation of the portable electroencephalography (EEG) device. In doing so, the brainwave readings from four participants at the Tuanku Mizan Zainal Abidin Mosque were observed. Data from the EEG device in the form of brainwave signals was analysed through the performance metrics detection suite which focused on the possibility of analysing brainwave data through three phases of habitation. The findings detected relaxation performance metrics from the participants whilst being within the mosque prayer area, whereas the phases prior to entering and after leaving the mosque appears to have detected higher excitement and engagement levels. Thus, it could be deduced that the interior prayer area of the mosque appears to have had a positive influence on the participant's physiology. This study could contribute to the novel field of neuroarchitecture in Malaysia, an area of study at the threshold of neuroscience and architecture that could be significant in understanding the relationship between the built environment and human physiology.
methodology: This study employed a triangulation methodology, combining quantitative (neuroscience data) and qualitative (interview) methods. It was a single case study focusing on the Tuanku Mizan Zainal Abidin Mosque (Iron Mosque) in Putrajaya, Malaysia. Brainwave signals were recorded in real-time using a portable Emotiv Insight 5 Channel Mobile EEG Device. Participants were seated quietly with eyes open for three separate phases of five minutes each: outside the prayer space (before), inside the prayer space (during), and outside the prayer space again (after). Data was collected via screenshots of the MyEmotiv application's Mental Performance Metrics. Qualitative feedback was gathered through brief focus group interviews the day after the experiment.
sample: Four (4) participants (2 males, M1 & M2; 2 females, F1 & F2) from the Built Environment discipline. All participants were Muslim and were visiting the mosque for the first time.
manipulated_features: The study investigated the impact of the 'interior prayer area' of a mosque, specifically the Tuanku Mizan Zainal Abidin Mosque, on human physiology. Architectural elements mentioned in qualitative feedback include: high ceiling, multiple smaller entrances, views towards a water feature, materials on the floor (cool to the touch), scale, and volume of space.
outcomes: Human physiological and mental responses were measured. Quantitative outcomes included brainwave signals, specifically Mental Performance Metrics (excitement, engagement, relaxation, interest, stress, focus) detected by the Emotiv Insight device. Qualitative outcomes included participants' reported feelings and experiences (joy, serenity, surprise, amazement, calmness, feeling small, feeling overwhelmed, problems being insignificant).

Whilst being within the mosque prayer area (2nd interval), all participants recorded dominant relaxation frequencies:
After leaving the mosque prayer area (3rd interval), participants returned to exhibiting dominant excitement or engagement frequencies:
The frequency of engagement and excitement in the 3rd interval was lower than in the 1st interval, possibly attributed to the sense of relaxation experienced in the 2nd interval.
Qualitative feedback indicated participants felt 'joy, serenity, surprise, and amazement' within the mosque interior.
Participants reported feelings of calmness and tranquility within the mosque.
Specific design factors like high ceilings, multiple entrances, water features, and tactile floor materials were perceived to contribute to positive emotions and a sense of calm.
The scale and volume of the mosque space made participants feel 'small', 'God is big', 'problems were small and insignificant', and 'overwhelmed' in a positive, contemplative way.
theories_referenced: Phenomenology (Edmund Husserl): 'to live is to experience', conscious understanding of the world through sensory interactions, study of structures of consciousness as experienced from the first-person point of view.
Neuroarchitecture: fusion of neuroscience and architecture.
Logical Positivism (contrasted with phenomenology): quantitative and experimental methods to test hypothetical-deductive generalisations.
Prospect-Refuge theory (implied by reference to Frank Lloyd Wright's houses and 'refuge' and 'prospect' notions).
mechanisms: The paper suggests that human beings are connected to the world through sensory stimuli, and architectural design can modulate brain function and behavior. The brain scans the environment through senses, generating behaviors in response to stimuli. Arousal is linked to the body issuing chemicals that stimulate emotions and create physical agitation. Specific design factors (scale, tactile qualities, water elements) are proposed to impact participants' emotions and physiological states, leading to relaxation or engagement.
limitations: The actual time to adjust sensors and calibrate equipment was much longer than the planned 15 minutes per participant.
Moments occurred during recording where sensors detached, producing 'noise' glitches in readings.
Small sampling size: four (4) participants in one (1) mosque.
The study is theoretical and exploratory, not intended as a generic tool for broader conclusions or statistical generalization.
design_implications: The findings suggest that specific architectural elements and the overall design of religious spaces like mosques can positively influence human physiology and emotional well-being, promoting relaxation.
Neuroscience data can provide evidence-based insights for designing built environments that promote well-being.
Understanding the link between space, brain, logic, intuition, architectural design, and human emotions can lead to a new frontier of phenomenological neuroarchitecture.
Designers should consider elements like scale, views to nature/water, and tactile materials to evoke specific emotional and physiological responses (e.g., calmness, contemplation).
